items.why: The viewer recognizes the legal property deed as the opening focus.
The board only shows Transylvania entering and dimming beside the deed without conveying the gloomy castle room or flickering lamp shadows.
The room setting, deed icon, and text convey the parchment sliding toward a hand.
The reaching figure and text accurately convey the strange hand with hair on the palm.
Using a versus layout leads the viewer to think Dracula is confronting the deed rather than signing it.
Stamping MISREAD on the deed leaves it vague whether the deed itself or the invasion is what has been misread.
An empty refute diagram signals a refutation is starting without showing the classic horror tropes being challenged.
The unlabeled refute diagram fails to convey the thesis that filing, not faith or courage, defeats Dracula.
The blank refute diagram gives no indication that diaries, bills, and telegrams form the evidentiary case.
The text and worried poses depict people who faced the horror but miss the speaker rejecting the paperwork premise.
The reaching protagonists, shield icon, and text convey fighting the horror with crucifixes and stakes.
The smirking aristocrat and text accurately convey that paperwork cannot kill a warlord.
The title and growing deed correctly introduce Exhibit 1, the deed to Carfax.
The layout and label establish Jonathan as an English solicitor arriving in Transylvania.
Moving Jonathan apart from Transylvania makes the viewer think he left Transylvania instead of being isolated inside it away from civilization.
Generic act and change tokens do not show that Jonathan presents the deed and Dracula signs it.
Joining Dracula with the deed toward London and the title accurately convey that his first act is a signature.
The labels and growing Dracula convey both his entry via property law and his underlying menace.
Dimming the deed while Dracula grows accurately conveys that the signature is secondary to his physical threat.
Staging Dracula reaching angrily over a cowering Jonathan depicts a face-to-face intimidation instead of Dracula crawling down the castle's outer walls.
The towering monster beside the deed icon and text captures that a legal contract means nothing to him.
Lining up Dracula, the deed, and Jonathan with the JUST A SHOW stamp conveys the pantomime of commerce.
Jonathan holding notes beside Carfax with its layout label captures his detailed journal description of the property.
The labels directly communicate the twenty-acre estate enclosed by an ancient stone wall.
Dimming and expanding Carfax around the chapel label captures its gloomy grounds and crucial ruined chapel.
Bringing Dracula and the fifty labeled earth boxes into Carfax conveys why he needs the enclosed space.
Crossing out the deed while restoring Carfax and the earth boxes implies the estate works without the contract rather than failing without it.
Dracula holding the deed, paying coins, and Carfax stamped SOLD convey that he legally buys his fortress.
The growing deed, SECURED stamp, and title capture that the beachhead is legally secured on paper.
The menacing aristocrat beside the deed icon and question text accurately convey the doubt over whether a lease can stop him.
The title and growing atlas clearly introduce Exhibit 2, the atlas with three rings.
Pairing Jonathan with Transylvania and a generic change cue omits that he finds a library full of books about England.
Jonathan interacting with the growing atlas captures him finding and examining the English atlas.
The labeled London and Whitby locations on the expanding atlas convey the marked targets.
Pairing the atlas with a growing timetable captures the railway guide and directories sitting beside it.
Dracula working over the atlas and timetable under the meticulous clerk label captures the claim directly.
Dracula using the timetable to strike London conveys his weaponization of British transit data.
The title and labels on the atlas and timetable capture Dracula plotting a logistical network into London.
The angry aristocrat and text accurately signal a challenge to the clerk interpretation.
The battlefield icon and text reframe Dracula as a centuries-old warlord.
Generic grow, act, and dim motions against the atlas fail to convey that Dracula is out of his depth in the nineteenth century.
Separating Dracula from the atlas while crowning and growing him conveys his ancient conquering bloodline.
Uncrowning Dracula as he shifts beside Jonathan makes him appear diminished and muddles the transition into his library speech.
Crowning and growing Dracula alongside London captures his desire to rule as master.
Setting aside the crown and merging with London conveys his wish to blend in like everyone else.
Dracula transforming and merging directly with London captures him adapting to pass unnoticed.
Dracula taking the atlas and covering himself behind it conveys using data as camouflage.
Holding the atlas under the masked ancient evil label directly matches the narration.
The secured deed and Dracula covering himself again summarize how paperwork secures his arrival and data hides him.
The smirking aristocrat and text capture the pivot to Dracula defying all logic.
Focusing on the mirror with the May 8 morning date directly introduces Exhibit 3.
Triggering a change cue on Jonathan makes him appear to react to something rather than calmly shaving.
Dracula appearing close beside a startled Jonathan as focus snaps to the mirror captures the moment.
Covering Dracula with the no-reflection label while Jonathan bursts captures the shock of the empty mirror.
Uncovering and growing Dracula without any cue for blood or fury leaves the cause of his reaction vague.
Putting the burst effect on Jonathan makes it look like Jonathan recoils from Dracula instead of Dracula lunging and recoiling from the crucifix.
Dracula taking the mirror and the shattered-on-the-stones title convey him throwing it out the window.
The stopped aristocrat, shield icon, and text capture the physical power of the crucifix.
The surprised gentleman, shield, and text convey that faith and the crucifix stopped a lethal attack.
Jonathan shaking beside the mirror while Dracula stays covered captures both the rebuttal title and Jonathan's panic over the missing reflection.
A generic act cue on Jonathan gives no indication that he is writing the event down in his journal.
Labeling the mirror as a diary that uncovers Dracula captures how the journal becomes proof of the monster.
Acting and shaking without any diary or notes visual show panic without conveying ink as a coping mechanism.
Showing Jonathan working on notes omits the crucifix rebuttal and leaves unclear what his desperate entry contains.
Jonathan holding a book under the bare-meager-facts label accurately matches the narration.
The frightened gentleman clutching notes with the text captures reducing the horror to data to keep his sanity.
The causal chain directly links having no reflection to creating a paper trail.
The completed diagram chain captures how turning the missing reflection into a paper trail saves sanity.
The shaking ship and growing logbook introduce Exhibit 4 and the question of whether a log can save a crew at sea.
The date and shaking Demeter arriving at Whitby capture the ship's storm-tossed entry into the harbor.
The shuddering, dimming ship with the dead-captain label matches the Coast Guard discovery.
Focusing on the logbook emerging from the Demeter captures the discovery of the bottled roll of paper.
Crossing out the ship while the logbook grows captures that the written record outlives physical survival.
An earth box colliding with the Demeter beside the logbook conveys the cargo that doomed the ship.
Focusing on the fifty earth boxes and logbook misses the crucial pivot to the crucifix tied in the dead captain's hands.
Dracula halting before the shield and HOLY STAND text captures the captain's spiritual defiance against the devil.
The Demeter shaking against Dracula while the logbook tracks a disappearing crew captures the inspector's reading.
The August 3 date aboard the Demeter and growing logbook introduce the climax of the ship's log.
Covering the ship with the title NO ONE AT THE WHEEL captures the thick fog and vanished helmsman.
A storm cloud icon by the shore with generic text leaves out the mad mate recounting creeping up on an intangible monster at sea.
Placing the earth box and words on the shore mislocates the shipboard scene and leaves out that the mate's knife attack failed.
The waves icon and text convey someone throwing himself into the sea.
The diagram chain directly summarizes that physical force hits empty space and makes violence useless.
Sealing the log in a bottle while crossing out both log and ship captures both the warning and its failure to save anyone.
Stamping the crossed-out logbook POST-MORTEM captures that it was only a coroner's report after the deaths.
Dimming the logbook and moving the ship next to Whitby captures the pivot to what happens on land.
Stamping the earth boxes LEGAL under Whitby's consignment papers captures Billington legally receiving the cargo.
Delivering the earth boxes to Whitby while the ship dims and is crossed out captures bureaucracy triumphing over the tragedy.
Stamping the Demeter DEATH alongside receipts and the surviving logbook summarizes the voyage's outcome.
Pairing the Demeter with receipts and bursting into London conveys the legally shielded threat spreading to London.
Growing Lucy's medical chart alongside Lucy changing introduces Exhibit 5 and the medical perspective.
Showing Lucy versus London with London covered fails to convey her closed London bedroom at night.
Grouping Helsing, Seward, and Lucy under the title conveys the experimental blood transfusions.
Flowing from Seward, Quincey, and Helsing to Lucy with the label captures four men's blood being transfused into her.
Seward acting beside Lucy's chart under the title conveys him recording everything on his medical chart.
Seward holding notes and labeling the chart with physical symptoms matches him logging her condition.
Covering Lucy's chart while Seward acts leaves it ambiguous whether the chart is blind to reality or being deliberately hidden.
Stamping Lucy's chart MERE ANEMIA while Seward takes notes and Lucy worsens captures science missing the curse.
Helsing uncovering and growing the medical chart captures how the data sparks his realization.
Helsing examining Lucy labeled with four men's blood captures his observation of the transfusions.
The title WHAT TOOK IT OUT beside the chart and dimming Lucy conveys the mathematical proof of a supernatural drain.
Dracula acting against a dimming Lucy under A FAILING BATTLE captures the monster feeding on her.
Crossing out both and stamping the chart NO CURE conveys that the records could not heal or save her.
Dimming the chart as Lucy changes under A HUGE DOUBT summarizes the failure of medical measurement.
The diagram chain directly links failing science to turning toward ancient superstitions.
Growing the garlic window under the title directly introduces Exhibit 6.
Helsing acting to enlarge the garlic window around Lucy captures him bringing garlic to protect her room.
Helsing holding flowers while enlarging the garlic barrier around Lucy conveys securing the room and wreath.
Helsing acting with the title DO NOT DISTURB IT captures his strict warning.
Shaking and dimming the garlic window without Mrs. Westenra present omits that Lucy's mother opened the window and removed the garlic.
Crossing out the garlic window and stamping it HUMAN BREACH captures that human interference undid the defense.
Restoring the garlic window while keeping it apart from a dimming Lucy captures that removing an effective ward doomed her.
Crossing out the garlic window as Dracula acts and grows conveys that breaking the ward invited the monster back.
Breaking the garlic ward as Dracula joins together with Lucy captures her falling back under his control.
The garlic window growing before dimming and crossing out captures a real ward tragically subverted.
Aligning Dracula, Lucy, and the dimmed garlic window under AN AGONIZING DOUBT captures the fallen defense.
Growing Lucy's memo under the title introduces Exhibit 7 as Lucy's final human act.
Shaking Lucy surrounded by Helsing, Seward, and Quincey conveys the chaotic scene after the final attack.
Showing only Lucy dimming opposite Helsing omits the drugged maids and dead mother.
Lucy's memo entering and growing between Helsing and Lucy captures the discovery of the hidden paper.
Lucy holding onto her growing memo conveys that she wrote and hid an account of what happened.
Stamping the memo held by Lucy as TESTIMONY captures her final act of leaving a witness record.
Crossing out the dropped memo and stamping Lucy MONSTER captures her death and transformation.
A violent clash between Helsing and Lucy while the memo is crossed out captures physical action stopping her where paper failed.
Stamping the memo MASSIVE THREAT as Helsing takes and puts it away conveys him seizing and hiding it.
Helsing and Seward standing together to cover and cross out the memo captures concealing it from outsiders.
The memo growing and bursting under REAL EVIDENCE conveys the explosive legal exposure it poses.
The worried men putting the letter away under SUPPRESSED HER ARCHIVE matches the narration directly.
The worried physician beside notes and the question text conveys the doubt over how to weaponize hidden secrets.
Mina facing the typewriter labeled Exhibit 8 directly introduces Mina's typewriter.
The labels for shorthand journal, wax cylinders, and mountain of formats capture the varied media pile.
Mina acting under ONE CHRONOLOGICAL FILE captures her transcribing and organizing all the records.
Mina holding collated notes while Dracula dims under DEFEATED BY COLLATION matches the turning point claim.
Mina typing and bringing the fifty boxes of earth into view conveys the timeline revealing the boxes.
Dimming the typewriter under JUST A MACHINE conveys the skepticism that it only processes words.
The angry man pointing at Dracula with CONFRONT THE MONSTER captures the argument for physical courage.
Crossing out the typewriter against knives under NOT A WEAPON and its bravery-record label matches the narration.
Quincey holding notes under SEE THE BIG PICTURE conveys reading the typed manuscript and understanding the whole threat.
Connecting the ghost ship Demeter, Renfield, and Carfax under CONNECTING THE DOTS matches the narration directly.
Showing only a change cue on Mina under October 3 omits that the men are out hunting the boxes while she sleeps in her bedroom.
